pages.title: Central business logic
pages.headline: Cardiology needs the details; a pilot is cheap.
pages.sub: The same two sentences as slide 9 of the Maker Day 2 deck, word for word.

blocks.text: People will buy it because cardiology guidelines need which relative and what age, intake forms take it from memory, and for $500 per cardiologist a year a practice-sent link puts those details, sourced, in the chart before visit one.

We can make it because the patient side already runs on open health standards, a PDF reaches any chart, and a pilot on vendors that sign HIPAA contracts costs under $850 a month, which 17–21 paying cardiologists cover, founders unpaid.

pages.footer: Evidence: Step 4 (guidelines, intake forms, practice-sent links), Step 5 (open standards, PDF, $689–834 a month). Payment and relatives' answers are untested.

items.text: **1. A practice pays** $500 per cardiologist a year despite free intake tools.
**2. Staff time is saved:** a 2026 trial found no shorter counseling time [S9].
**3. Patients finish pre-visit** when a US cardiology practice sends the link.
**4. Relatives respond:** 29% dropped out at the invite step elsewhere [93].
**5. Cardiologists trust and act on the page:** none interviewed; D021, a genetics counselor, doubts patient-built pedigrees.
**6. The page fits the practice's EHR workflow:** their EHRs are unknown.
**15 patients;** only ID007 is a cardiology patient.
**6 clinicians:** an internist, a nurse, 2 physician assistants, an ER doctor (ID010), a genetics counselor (D021).
**Gap: 0 practice managers, 0 cardiologists, 0 relatives.** All 21 come from our September diagnosis research.

pages.footer: Unproven, ranked 7th: our four differences beat FamGenix enough to matter (no hands-on test yet). Interviews: our course log (Team Hub).
